lines.text: Your crush just said no. In front of the whole school.
You're standing on a cafeteria table, holding flowers. 300 phones are filming.
Bro. Get down. Please get down.
And you're smiling. Because today doesn't count.
Midnight. Everything rewinds. Same morning. Same alarm. Same Monday.
Nobody remembers the table. Nobody but you.
Starting today, you live every day twice. First a practice run. Then the real one. In 30 days you'll be a millionaire, go viral, and face the one moment you can't practice for.
The rules. Take 1: nothing counts. At midnight, it's erased. Take 2: everything is real.
So in take 2, you skip the table.
Hey, Ava. Cool backpack.
Thanks. No flowers today?
What?
Nothing.
Strange thing to say. Remember it.
Tuesday, take 1. A surprise math test. You fail it, and memorize every question.
Tuesday, take 2. 100 percent. Your teacher checks your sleeves.
And take 1 becomes the best part of your life. Nothing counts. So you drive a golf cart through the hallway. You eat 9 burgers. You tell the principal what you really think of his tie.
Who are you today?
Doesn't matter. You won't remember.
Then YouTube shows you a guy opening 1,000 packs of trading cards, hunting for one rare card. In February 2026, Logan Paul's Pikachu Illustrator card sold for 16.5 million dollars. One card.
The card shop near school has 40 sealed packs. Take 1: you spend your savings, 200 dollars, and open every single one.
Pack 31. A card worth 2,800 dollars.
Take 2: you walk in with 5 dollars.
Just this one, please.
Lucky guess, kid.
Next, the lottery. Your mom plays your 6 numbers. Every single one misses.
In 1961, a scientist named Edward Lorenz rounded one number in a weather simulation, from 0.506127 to 0.506. The whole forecast changed. Lottery balls never bounce the same way twice.
New rule. Chance changes. Whatever is already sealed stays the same.
Sealed. Like storage units. You've seen the videos: people pay 300 dollars for an abandoned unit without knowing what's inside.
Take 1: you watch all 12 doors open. Unit 7: a 1980s arcade machine. Take 2: Theo's brother bids on one door only.
Why 7?
Feeling.
The arcade machine sells for 9,000 dollars. Theo posts the video: This kid only picks winners. 6 million views.
By week 3: 41,000 dollars. And one email.
But take 1 is changing you. One morning, in a practice run, you snap at your mom. Something you'd never say. It's fine. It's a draft.
Take 2. She makes you pancakes. She doesn't remember. You do.
At least nobody else sees your drafts. That's what you think.
Another take 1. You skip school, and find Ava at the aquarium. Alone. Watching the octopus.
Octopus blood is blue. Copper instead of iron. Also, 3 hearts.
Why do you know that?
Why are you skipping school?
It's the best hour of your month. And at midnight, it never happened.
The email. The 1 Million Dollar Question. A live show, 20 million viewers. One contestant. One question, sealed in an envelope a week before.
Sealed. You almost laugh.
The plan. Take 1: hear the question. Take 2: answer it.
Saturday, take 1. 8:00 p.m. The envelope opens.
Which planet has the longest day?
Uh... Jupiter?
Venus. I'm so sorry.
You're not. You walk off stage smiling. Then your phone rings.
Your mom was driving to the studio to surprise you. 7:42 p.m. A truck ran a red light. She's in surgery.
You sit in the hospital and wait for midnight.
Take 2. 7:30 p.m. You call her.
Mom, don't leave yet. I can't find my lucky socks.
Your what?
You keep her on the phone for 14 minutes. The truck runs the red light at an empty intersection.
But you walk on stage 14 minutes late. The show started without you. A backup contestant got your envelope.
No problem. We'll open a new one.
A question you've never heard. 30 seconds. 1 million dollars. And no take 2.
What color is an octopus's blood?
A Tuesday that never happened.
Blue.
That is... correct!
1 million dollars. Theo screams. Your mom is in row 3. Crying. Fine.
Backstage, Ava is waiting.
Told you. Copper.
You told me that in a take 1. You can't remember that.
I remember the table, too. Nice flowers.
She's lived every day twice since she was 9.
Then why did you say no?
It was a draft. Ask me on a day that counts.
If you lived every day twice, what would you do on the day that doesn't count?
